name: Trace an assignment
sub: Follow the value at each line
rule: In x ← expression, evaluate the right side using the current values. Copy the result into x. Each later line starts with the values the previous line left behind.
trick: Give each variable its own column. When one variable changes, leave the others alone. The practice questions also write the arrow as <-.

examples.note: spares still holds the 9 it copied.
The right side uses 9. The new value of tiles is 11.

another.text: Copy the score from the scoreboard onto a ticket. The ticket keeps that score even when the scoreboard changes.
another.example: Copy 8 onto your ticket. If the board goes to 10, your ticket still says 8.

steps.ask: After the first line, what is blue?
steps.hint: Follow the arrow from the value to the name.
Use the current value of blue in blue + 4.

steps.ask: After the final line, what are blue and gold?
steps.hint: The final arrow points to blue.
steps.line: blue holds 8 and gold still holds 7

questions.stem: After a ← 5, b ← a, then a ← 13, what does b hold?
After total ← 6, extra ← 2, then total ← total - extra, what does total hold?
questions.why: The right side evaluates to 6 - 2, which is 4.

name: Evaluate a Boolean condition
rule: A comparison gives true or false. AND needs both conditions to be true. OR needs at least one. NOT reverses a Boolean value. IF runs its first block when the condition is true and its ELSE block when it is false.
trick: Substitute the values, evaluate each comparison, then combine the results. In a sequence of separate IF statements, test each condition when you reach it.

examples.note: With seats equal to 6, the first comparison is true and the second is false. The result is false.
With color equal to "blue", the comparison is false and NOT makes the result true.

another.text: A game opens one gate if you have both tickets. Another gate opens if you have either ticket.
another.example: With just the blue ticket, blue AND yellow is false. Blue OR yellow is true.

steps.ask: With points equal to 8, is points > 5 true?

steps.hint: AND needs two true values, so follow ELSE.
steps.line: true AND false gives false. The program displays 2.

questions.stem: Which value of t makes (t ≥ 4) AND (t < 7) true?
questions.why: 6 meets both limits. The upper limit excludes 7.
The OR gives false. NOT reverses it to true.

name: Evaluate arithmetic and MOD
sub: Distinguish a quotient from a remainder
rule: In AP pseudocode, / gives a quotient, which can be a decimal. For a nonnegative integer a and a positive integer b, a MOD b gives the remainder. Work inside parentheses first, then evaluate *, / and MOD from left to right before + and -.
trick: Find the largest whole multiple of b that fits in a. Subtract it from a to get the remainder.

examples.note: Three groups of 4 use 12. The remainder is 2, so the expression gives 3.

another.text: If everyone needs a full pair of gloves, the remainder counts the gloves left without a partner.
another.example: Nine gloves make four pairs and leave one glove. 9 MOD 2 is 1.

steps.hint: MOD has the same precedence as multiplication.

steps.ask: What remains after grouping 23 into sixes?

questions.why: The division operator returns the quotient, including its fractional part.

name: Trace a loop
sub: Track the value after each repetition
rule: REPEAT n TIMES runs its body n times. REPEAT UNTIL checks its condition before each repetition and stops when it is true. FOR EACH visits the elements of a list in order. Each repetition uses the values left by the previous one.
trick: Write the starting value, then add one row per repetition. For a condition-controlled loop, check the stopping condition before adding another row.

examples.text:
total ← 0
FOR EACH v IN [2, 7] { total ← total + v }
examples.note: The running total goes from 0 to 2 to 9.

another.text: Move a game piece three spaces each turn. Stop as soon as it reaches or passes the finish square.
another.example: Starting at 1 with a finish at 6, you land on 4, then 7. There is no third move.

steps.ask: At the start, should the body run?
steps.hint: The stopping condition is still false at 2.

steps.ask: What does n hold after one repetition?
steps.line: n is 5, so another repetition starts

steps.ask: What value does n hold when the loop ends?
steps.hint: Add 3 once more and check the condition.
steps.line: n is 8. The stopping condition is true.

questions.stem: n starts at 4. REPEAT 2 TIMES { n ← n + 5 }. What is n afterward?
questions.why: The two repetitions produce 9 and then 14.

questions.stem: n starts at 8. How often does REPEAT UNTIL (n > 5) { n ← n + 1 } run its body?
questions.why: 8 > 5 is already true at the first check.

name: Read and update list positions
sub: Count the first element as position 1
rule: AP list indices start at 1 and end at LENGTH(list). INSERT puts a new item at the specified position and shifts later items right. REMOVE deletes the item at that position and shifts the following items left.
trick: Write the positions above the list. After an insertion or removal, number the resulting list again before reading an item.

examples.note: The result is [3, 4, 5, 8]. The original second item moves to position 3.

another.text: Number the runners in a line from first to last. If the first runner leaves, the runner who was second moves into first place.
another.example: In the line Jo, Sal, Bo, the second runner is Sal.

steps.hint: Delete the item at the specified position.
Count to the second item in the new list.

questions.stem: For a ← [1, 4, 6], which list results from INSERT(a, 2, 9)?
questions.why: 9 takes position 2. The existing 4 and 6 shift one place right.
